notes.front: What is a Safety Data Sheet (SDS)?
notes.back: A form giving the detailed breakdown of a material’s chemicals, including formulas and the action to take after contact.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it a more detailed version of the chemical safety issues.
notes.example: Like the warning label on a tin of paint stripper, but a full sheet: the label gives the quick picture, the SDS gives the chemistry and what to do if it gets on you.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: The SDS is a more detailed version of the chemical safety issues. These forms have the detailed breakdown of the chemicals, including formulas and action to take if personnel come in contact with the chemicals.

notes.front: What is foreign object damage (FOD)?
notes.back: Any damage to aircraft, personnel or equipment caused by any loose object.
notes.explanation: The loose object can be anything: the handbook’s examples include broken runway concrete, shop towels and safety wire.
notes.example: Like a stone flicked up into a car windscreen, but on a ramp the “stone” may be a forgotten rag or rivet stem.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Foreign Object Damage (FOD)”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Foreign object damage (FOD) is any damage to aircraft, personnel, or equipment caused by any loose object. These loose objects can be anything, such as broken runway concrete, shop towels, safety wire, etc.

notes.front: What does this deck mean by the fire triangle?
notes.back: The three things a fire needs: fuel, heat and oxygen.
notes.explanation: The handbook says that removing any one of the three puts the fire out.
notes.example: Like a three-legged stool: kick away any one leg and it falls over.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Requirements for Fire to Occur”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Three things are required for a fire. Remove any one of these things and the fire extinguishes: 1. Fuel—combines with oxygen in the presence of heat, releasing more heat. As a result, it reduces itself to other chemical compounds. 2. Heat—accelerates the combining of oxygen with fuel, in turn releasing more heat. 3. Oxygen—the element

notes.front: What is a Class A fire?
notes.back: A fire in ordinary combustible materials, such as wood, cloth, paper or upholstery.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three basic types into which the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) classifies fires for commercial purposes.
notes.example: Like a garden bonfire of branches and newspaper, but indoors in a hangar or workshop.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: For commercial purposes, the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) has classified fires into three basic types: Class A, Class B, and Class C. 1. Class A fires involve ordinary combustible materials, such as wood, cloth, paper, upholstery materials, and so forth.

notes.front: What is a Class B fire?
notes.back: A fire in flammable petroleum products or other flammable or combustible liquids, greases, solvents or paints.
notes.explanation: The NFPA places it second of its three basic fire types, after ordinary combustibles.
notes.example: Like a pool of spilled lighter fluid catching light, but the liquid might be a solvent or a paint.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 2. Class B fires involve flammable petroleum products or other flammable or combustible liquids, greases, solvents, paints, and so forth.

notes.front: What is a Class C fire?
notes.back: A fire involving energised electrical wiring and equipment.
notes.explanation: It is the third of the NFPA’s three basic fire types.
notes.example: Like a smoking extension lead that is still plugged in and live.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 3. Class C fires involve energized electrical wiring and equipment. A fourth class of fire, the Class D fire, involves flammable metal.

notes.front: What is a Class D fire?
notes.back: A fire involving flammable metal.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it a fourth class, which the NFPA does not commercially treat as a basic type.
notes.example: Like a firework sparkler’s metal burning white-hot, but on the scale of an aircraft part.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: A fourth class of fire, the Class D fire, involves flammable metal. Class D fires are not commercially considered by the NFPA to be a basic type of fire

notes.front: What is an auxiliary power unit (APU)?
notes.back: Generally a smaller turbine engine that provides compressed air for starting engines, cabin heating and cooling, and electrical power on the ground.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes its operation as normally simple.
notes.example: Like the generator on a camper van, but a small turbine that also supplies compressed air.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Auxiliary Power Units (APUs)”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: APUs are generally smaller turbine engines that provide compressed air for starting engines, cabin heating and cooling, and electrical power while on the ground. Their operation is normally simple.

notes.front: What is a hot start?
notes.back: A turbine start in which the engine starts but the exhaust gas temperature exceeds specified limits.
notes.explanation: The handbook says it is usually caused by an excessively rich air-fuel mixture entering the combustion chamber.
notes.example: Like a car whose temperature needle races into the red as soon as it starts, but the needle is exhaust gas temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hot Start”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: A hot start occurs when the engine starts, but the exhaust gas temperature exceeds specified limits. This is usually caused by an excessively rich air-fuel mixture entering the combustion chamber.

notes.front: What is a hung start?
notes.back: A turbine start in which the engine starts normally but rpm stays at a low value instead of rising to normal starting rpm.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it a false or hung start and says to shut the engine down.
notes.example: Like a lawnmower that catches but never picks up speed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “False or Hung Start”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: False or hung starts occur when the engine starts normally, but the rpm remains at some low value rather than increasing to the normal starting rpm. This is often the result of insufficient power to the starter or the starter cutting off before the engine starts self-accelerating. In this case, shut the engine down.

notes.front: In turbine starting, what does “engine fails to start” mean?
notes.back: The engine does not start within the prescribed time limit.
notes.explanation: Causes the handbook lists include lack of fuel, little or no electrical power to the ignition exciter, and incorrect fuel mixture.
notes.example: Like a car that cranks and cranks without firing, but with a set time limit on the attempt.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Engine Fails to Start”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: The engine failing to start within the prescribed time limit can be caused by lack of fuel to the engine, insufficient or no electrical power to the exciter in the ignition system, or incorrect fuel mixture.

notes.front: What is a ground power unit (GPU)?
notes.back: Ground support equipment that supplies electrical power to an aircraft; the movable type generally has an onboard engine turning a generator.
notes.explanation: Some smaller units use a series of batteries instead of an engine and generator.
notes.example: Like plugging a caravan into a campsite hook-up, but the hook-up is wheeled to the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Electric Ground Power Units”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: The movable type ground power unit (GPU) generally has an onboard engine that turns a generator to produce power. Some smaller units use a series of batteries.

notes.front: What is a hydraulic ground power unit?
notes.back: A unit, sometimes called a hydraulic mule, that provides hydraulic pressure to operate aircraft systems during maintenance.
notes.explanation: Portable test stands range from limited units to ones that can do every test a fixed-shop stand is designed to do.
notes.example: Like a car jack’s pump, but feeding pressure into the aircraft’s own hydraulic systems so they can be worked on the ground.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hydraulic Ground Power Units”, p. 1-22
notes.evidence: Portable hydraulic test stands are manufactured in many sizes and cost ranges. [Figure 1-29] Some have a limited range of operation, while others can be used to perform all the system tests that fixed-shop test stands are designed to perform. Hydraulic power units, sometimes called a hydraulic mule, provide hydraulic pressure to operate the aircraft systems during maintenance.

notes.front: What is a ground support air unit (air cart)?
notes.back: A cart supplying low-pressure, high-volume air (up to 50 psi) for starting engines and for heating and cooling the aircraft on the ground.
notes.explanation: The air works through the aircraft’s onboard systems, and the cart generally contains an APU.
notes.example: Like the aircraft’s own APU, but mounted on a cart and wheeled up from outside.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Ground Support Air Units”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: Air carts are used to provide low-pressure (up to 50 psi high volume flow) air that can be used for starting the engines and heating and cooling the aircraft on the ground (using the onboard aircraft systems). It generally consists of an APU

notes.front: In the Aviation Mechanic ACS, which subject area lists “fuel additives commonly used in the field” as a knowledge element?
notes.back: General Subject F, Ground Operations and Servicing.
notes.explanation: In that list it sits between the elements on fuel characteristics and identification and on the use of approved fuel grades.
notes.example: Like the element on approved fuel grades, but about substances added to fuel rather than the grade of the fuel itself.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), I.F Ground Operations and Servicing, p. 9
notes.evidence: AM.I.F.K9 Characteristics of aviation gasoline and turbine fuels, including basic types and means of identification. AM.I.F.K10 Fuel additives commonly used in the field. AM.I.F.K11 Use of approved grades/types of fuel in aircraft engines.
introduces: fuel additives commonly used in the field
uses: fuel additives commonly used in the field

notes.front: Why can a power cord with several broken inner wires start a fire?
notes.back: Current through the remaining wires rises, producing more heat than their insulation is designed to withstand.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s remedy is to monitor electrical equipment closely and repair or replace damaged items before further use.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fire Safety”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: When several wires inside a power cord are broken, the current passing through the remaining wires increases. This generates more heat than the insulation coatings on the wire are designed to withstand and can lead to a fire. Closely monitor the condition of electrical equipment. Repair or replace damaged equipment before further use.

notes.front: Electricity passing through the body can cause severe burns where it enters and leaves, and can damage or destroy the {{c1::nervous system}}.
notes.explanation: The handbook asks technicians for a working knowledge of electrical principles and a healthy respect for electricity’s capacity to do both work and damage.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Physiological Safety”, p. 1-1
notes.evidence: In addition, the nervous system is affected and can be damaged or destroyed. To safely deal with electricity, the technician must have a working knowledge of the principles of electricity and a healthy respect for its capability to do both work and damage.

notes.front: How large should a grinder’s wheel flanges and compression washer be?
notes.back: One-third the diameter of the wheel.
notes.explanation: It is one of the grinder checks, alongside never standing in the arc of the wheel in case it explodes.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Machine Tools”, p. 1-3
notes.evidence: Check the wheel flanges and compression washer. They should be one-third the diameter of the wheel. • Do not stand in the arc of the grinding wheel while operating in case the wheel explodes.

notes.front: When welding in a hangar, no aircraft are to be within {{c1::35 feet}} of the welding operation.
notes.explanation: The same list bars flammable material from the area around the welding operation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Machine Tools”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: No aircraft are to be within 35 feet of the welding operation. • No flammable material is permitted in the area around the welding operation.

notes.front: For welding in a hangar, what fire extinguishing equipment must be in the immediate area?
notes.back: Equipment with a minimum rating of 20B, with 80B-rated equipment as a backup.
notes.explanation: Trained fire watches are also to be present around the welding operation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Machine Tools”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Fire extinguishing equipment of a minimum rating of 20B must be in the immediate area with 80B rated equipment as a backup. • Trained fire watches are to be present in the area around the welding operation.

notes.front: A bracket must be welded on an aircraft inside the hangar. Another team wants to open a fuel tank on the same aircraft at the same time. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) Open fuel tanks and fuel system work are not permitted during welding
B) The tank may be opened if the aircraft is more than 35 feet away
C) The tank may be opened if a fire watch is present
D) Only painting is restricted during welding
notes.back: A) Open fuel tanks and fuel system work are not permitted during welding
notes.choicesExplained: C: a fire watch is required anyway, but it does not lift the ban on open tanks. B: the 35-foot rule is about other aircraft; here the tank is on the aircraft being welded. D: painting is banned too, but so is fuel work.
notes.explanation: During hangar welding the handbook forbids open fuel tanks and work on fuel systems, and painting too.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Machine Tools”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: During welding operations, open fuel tanks and work on fuel systems are not permitted. • Painting is not permitted.

notes.front: What must always be used when inflating tyres on any type of aircraft wheel?
notes.back: Tire cage guards.
notes.explanation: The one exception the handbook gives is adjusting the pressure of a tyre already installed on an aircraft; over-inflating high-pressure tyres can cause injury.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Compressed Gases”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: When inflating tires on any type of aircraft wheels, always use tire cage guards. Extreme caution is required to avoid over inflation of high-pressure tires because of possible personal injury.

notes.front: A technician needs to top up the pressure of a main-wheel tyre that is still fitted to the aircraft, using a high-pressure air bottle. Which statement matches the handbook?
notes.choices:
A) The wheel must be removed and placed in a tire cage first
B) Only nitrogen may be used, so the job cannot be done
C) No regulator is needed because the tyre is already installed
D) A tire cage is not required, and the bottle should have a pressure regulator
notes.back: D) A tire cage is not required, and the bottle should have a pressure regulator
notes.choicesExplained: A: cages are not required for adjusting pressure in an installed tyre. C: regulators on high-pressure bottles are what prevent over-inflation. B: the handbook sets no such restriction here.
notes.explanation: The handbook exempts tyres installed on the aircraft from the cage requirement, and asks for a regulator on high-pressure bottles to prevent over-inflation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Compressed Gases”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: Use pressure regulators on high-pressure air bottles to eliminate the possibility of over inflation of tires. Tire cages are not required when adjusting pressure in tires installed on an aircraft.

notes.front: What two things does a material safety (risk) diamond on a container tell a technician?
notes.back: The risk of the hazardous material inside, and, used properly with the tags, what personal safety equipment to use.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the risk diamond the most observable part of the SDS label.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: These diamond-shaped labels are a simple and quick way to determine the risk of hazardous material within the associated container and, if used properly with the tags, indicate what personal safety equipment to use. The most observable portion of the Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) (formerly known as Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS)) label is the risk diamond.

notes.front: A technician is about to use an unfamiliar solvent and wants the chemical formulas and what to do if it splashes on the skin. Where should they look?
notes.choices:
A) The Safety Data Sheet for the solvent
B) The marking on the nearest fire extinguisher
C) The title block of the aircraft drawing
D) The number in the risk diamond’s health block
notes.back: A) The Safety Data Sheet for the solvent
notes.choicesExplained: D: the diamond gives a quick 0–4 rating, not formulas or contact actions. B: extinguisher markings show fire classes. C: a drawing’s title block identifies the drawing, not chemical hazards.
notes.explanation: The SDS is the detailed document: it breaks down the chemicals, their formulas and the action to take after contact.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: The SDS is a more detailed version of the chemical safety issues. These forms have the detailed breakdown of the chemicals, including formulas and action to take if personnel come in contact with the chemicals.

notes.front: On a risk diamond, which hazard does the red segment represent?
notes.back: Flammability.
notes.explanation: Red is one of the three segments that carry a number from 0 to 4.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: It is a four-color segmented diamond that represents flammability (red), reactivity (yellow), health (blue), and special hazard (white). In the flammability, reactivity, and health blocks, there is a number from 0 to 4.

notes.front: On a risk diamond, which hazard does the yellow segment represent?
notes.back: Reactivity.
notes.explanation: Yellow, like red and blue, carries a number from 0 to 4.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: It is a four-color segmented diamond that represents flammability (red), reactivity (yellow), health (blue), and special hazard (white). In the flammability, reactivity, and health blocks, there is a number from 0 to 4.

notes.front: On a risk diamond, which hazard does the blue segment represent?
notes.back: Health.
notes.explanation: Blue is the last of the three numbered segments; the fourth segment is white.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: It is a four-color segmented diamond that represents flammability (red), reactivity (yellow), health (blue), and special hazard (white). In the flammability, reactivity, and health blocks, there is a number from 0 to 4.

notes.front: On a risk diamond, what does the white segment show?
notes.back: The special hazard, as a word or abbreviation.
notes.explanation: Examples the handbook gives are RAD for radiation, ALK for alkali materials and CARC for carcinogenic materials.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: The special hazard segment contains a word or abbreviation to represent the specific hazard. Some examples are RAD for radiation, ALK for alkali materials, Acid for acidic materials, and CARC for carcinogenic materials.

notes.front: A drum’s risk diamond shows 1 in blue, 0 in yellow and 3 in red. Which hazard is the most serious for this material?
notes.choices:
A) Health
B) Flammability
C) Reactivity
D) None: all three are within safe limits
notes.back: B) Flammability
notes.choicesExplained: A: blue is health, rated only 1. C: yellow is reactivity, rated 0. D: a 3 is close to the top of the scale, where 4 means very hazardous.
notes.explanation: On the 0–4 scale, 0 means little or no hazard and 4 means very hazardous, so the highest number marks the worst hazard.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Hazardous Materials”, p. 1-2
notes.evidence: Zero represents little or no hazard to the user, while 4 means that the material is very hazardous.

notes.front: What are the two types of hearing protection?
notes.back: External, such as earmuffs or headphones, and internal, which fits into the auditory canal.
notes.explanation: Both types reduce the sound level reaching the eardrum and so reduce the chances of hearing loss.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hearing Protection”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Hearing protection can be external or internal. Earmuffs or headphones are considered external protection. The internal type of hearing protection fits into the auditory canal. Both types reduce the sound level reaching the eardrum and reduce the chances of hearing loss.

notes.front: What are two measures the handbook gives for controlling FOD?
notes.back: Any two of: keep ramp and operation areas clean; a tool control program; convenient receptacles for used hardware, shop towels and other consumables.
notes.explanation: The handbook pairs these with a rule never to leave tools or other items around a turbine intake.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Foreign Object Damage (FOD)”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: To control FOD, keep ramp and operation areas clean, have a tool control program, and provide convenient receptacles for used hardware, shop towels, and other consumables. Never leave tools or other items around the intake of a turbine engine.

notes.front: Why must tools never be left around the intake of a turbine engine?
notes.back: The engine creates a low-pressure area in front of it that draws any loose object into the engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this a feature of the modern gas turbine engine.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Foreign Object Damage (FOD)”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Never leave tools or other items around the intake of a turbine engine. The modern gas turbine engine creates a low-pressure area in front of the engine that causes any loose object to be drawn into the engine.

notes.front: What FOD hazard does a turbine engine’s exhaust create?
notes.back: It can throw loose objects great distances with enough force to damage anything they hit.
notes.explanation: The handbook says a FOD program’s importance cannot be overstressed, given the cost of engines, components or a human life.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Foreign Object Damage (FOD)”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: The exhaust of these engines can propel loose objects great distances with enough force to damage anything that is hit. The importance of a FOD program cannot be overstressed when a technician considers the cost of engines, components, or a human life.

notes.front: After a job near a turbine engine, a mechanic drops safety-wire clippings on the ramp because there is no bin nearby. Which handbook FOD control is missing?
notes.choices:
A) Hearing protection
B) Convenient receptacles for used hardware and consumables
C) A risk diamond on the wire spool
D) Tire cage guards
notes.back: B) Convenient receptacles for used hardware and consumables
notes.choicesExplained: A: hearing protection guards against noise, not loose objects. C: risk diamonds label hazardous materials. D: tyre cages guard against tyre bursts during inflation.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s FOD controls include convenient receptacles for used hardware and other consumables, so that nothing is left loose.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Foreign Object Damage (FOD)”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: To control FOD, keep ramp and operation areas clean, have a tool control program, and provide convenient receptacles for used hardware, shop towels, and other consumables.

notes.front: Near a taxiing aircraft, what must a technician do instead of assuming the pilot can see them?
notes.back: Stay within the pilot’s view while on the ramp.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that turbine engine intakes and exhausts are also very hazardous areas.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Airplanes”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Technicians cannot assume the pilot of a taxiing aircraft can see them and must stay within the pilot’s view while on the ramp area. Turbine engine intakes and exhaust can also be very hazardous areas.

notes.front: A baggage cart is parked unbraked on a slight slope, right up against the wing of an aircraft with its engines running. What does the handbook require?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as long as the engines are only at idle
B) Space between cart and aircraft, and securing it against rolling
C) That the cart be moved behind the engine exhaust
D) Only that the cart carries a risk diamond
notes.back: B) Space between cart and aircraft, and securing it against rolling
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook sets no idle exception. D: risk diamonds are for hazardous materials. C: turbine exhaust is itself a hazardous area.
notes.explanation: Support equipment near aircraft needs space between it and the aircraft and must be secured so it cannot roll into the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Airplanes”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: When operating support equipment around aircraft, be sure to allow space between it and the aircraft, and secure it so it cannot roll into the aircraft. All items in the area of operating aircraft must be stowed properly.

notes.front: Why must a single-rotor helicopter never be approached from the rear?
notes.back: The tail rotor is invisible when operating.
notes.explanation: The handbook also says to cross from one side to the other around the nose, never around the tail.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Helicopters”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Never approach a single-rotor helicopter from the rear. The tail rotor is invisible when operating. • Never go from one side of the helicopter to the other by going around the tail. Always go around the nose of the helicopter.

notes.front: With the blades turning, a mechanic walks towards a helicopter carrying a long pitot-cover pole upright over one shoulder. What is the hazard the handbook names?
notes.choices:
A) The blades could hit the upright pole, damaging the blades and injuring the mechanic
B) The pole could be drawn into a turbine intake as FOD
C) The pilot cannot see anyone approaching from the front
D) Nothing, provided the approach is from the nose
notes.back: A) The blades could hit the upright pole, damaging the blades and injuring the mechanic
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook’s point here is blade strike, not ingestion. C: the handbook says to approach in view of the pilot, which the front allows. D: the height of the item is the danger, whatever the direction.
notes.explanation: The handbook forbids approaching with anything tall enough for the blades to hit, because of blade damage and injury.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Safety Around Helicopters”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: Never approach a helicopter carrying anything with a vertical height that the blades could hit. This could cause blade damage and injury to the individual.

notes.front: In the requirements for fire, which element combines with oxygen in the presence of heat, releasing more heat?
notes.back: Fuel.
notes.explanation: In doing so it reduces itself to other chemical compounds.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Requirements for Fire to Occur”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 1. Fuel—combines with oxygen in the presence of heat, releasing more heat. As a result, it reduces itself to other chemical compounds.

notes.front: In the requirements for fire, which element accelerates the combining of oxygen with fuel?
notes.back: Heat.
notes.explanation: In turn, the combining releases more heat.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Requirements for Fire to Occur”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 2. Heat—accelerates the combining of oxygen with fuel, in turn releasing more heat.

notes.front: In the requirements for fire, which element combines chemically with another substance through oxidation?
notes.back: Oxygen.
notes.explanation: Rapid oxidation with a noticeable release of heat and light is what the handbook calls combustion or burning.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Requirements for Fire to Occur”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 3. Oxygen—the element that combines chemically with another substance through the process of oxidation. Rapid oxidation, accompanied by a noticeable release of heat and light, is called combustion or burning.

notes.front: A CO2 extinguisher is used on a burning pile of rags. Which element of the fire triangle does it mainly remove?
notes.choices:
A) Fuel
B) Heat, and nothing else
C) Oxygen
D) None; CO2 only works on metal fires
notes.back: C) Oxygen
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rags are still there; CO2 does not remove fuel. B: CO2 does cool, but its main action is removing oxygen. D: the handbook says never use CO2 on Class D (metal) fires.
notes.explanation: The handbook says CO2 extinguishes a fire by depriving it of oxygen; it also cools the burning material.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguishers are used for Class A, B, and C fires, extinguishing the fire by depriving it of oxygen. [Figure 1-4] Additionally, like water-type extinguishers, CO2 cools the burning material.

notes.front: For commercial purposes, the NFPA classifies fires into {{c1::three}} basic types.
notes.explanation: The three basic types are Class A, Class B and Class C.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) has classified fires into three basic types: Class A, Class B, and Class C.

notes.front: Why does the NFPA not commercially treat Class D as a basic type of fire?
notes.back: Class D fires are caused by a Class A, B or C fire.
notes.explanation: The handbook says they usually involve magnesium in the shop or in wheels and brakes, or come from improper welding.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Class D fires are not commercially considered by the NFPA to be a basic type of fire since they are caused by a Class A, B, or C fire. Usually Class D fires involve magnesium in the shop, or in aircraft wheels and brakes, or are the result of improper welding operations.

notes.front: Wooden crates and cardboard packing in a hangar store catch fire. Which class of fire is it?
notes.choices:
A) Class B
B) Class A
C) Class D
D) Class C
notes.back: B) Class A
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class B is flammable liquids, greases, solvents and paints. D: Class C needs energised electrical equipment. C: Class D involves flammable metal.
notes.explanation: Wood and paper are ordinary combustible materials, which define a Class A fire.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 1. Class A fires involve ordinary combustible materials, such as wood, cloth, paper, upholstery materials, and so forth.

notes.front: A tray of cleaning solvent in the paint shop catches fire. Which class of fire is it?
notes.choices:
A) Class A
B) Class D
C) Class C
D) Class B
notes.back: D) Class B
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class A is ordinary combustibles such as wood and paper. C: Class C needs energised electrical equipment. B: Class D involves flammable metal.
notes.explanation: Flammable or combustible liquids such as solvents and paints define a Class B fire.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 2. Class B fires involve flammable petroleum products or other flammable or combustible liquids, greases, solvents, paints, and so forth.

notes.front: The insulation on a live ground power cable begins to burn while the unit is still supplying power. Which class of fire is it?
notes.choices:
A) Class D
B) Class A
C) Class C
D) Class B
notes.back: C) Class C
notes.choicesExplained: B: the wiring is energised, which makes it Class C, not an ordinary combustible fire. A: no flammable metal is burning. D: no flammable liquid is involved.
notes.explanation: Burning energised electrical wiring and equipment defines a Class C fire.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: 3. Class C fires involve energized electrical wiring and equipment.

notes.front: After a hard stop, a magnesium wheel on a light aircraft starts burning with an intense white flame. Which class of fire is it?
notes.choices:
A) Class A
B) Class D
C) Class B
D) Class C
notes.back: B) Class D
notes.choicesExplained: A: the burning material is metal, not an ordinary combustible. C: no flammable liquid is the fuel. D: nothing energised is burning.
notes.explanation: Flammable metal defines a Class D fire, and the handbook says these usually involve magnesium, including in wheels and brakes.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Classification of Fires”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: A fourth class of fire, the Class D fire, involves flammable metal. Class D fires are not commercially considered by the NFPA to be a basic type of fire since they are caused by a Class A, B, or C fire. Usually Class D fires involve magnesium in the shop, or in aircraft wheels and brakes

notes.front: Which type of extinguisher does the handbook call the best for Class A fires?
notes.back: Water.
notes.explanation: Water both deprives the fire of oxygen and cools the material being burned.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Water extinguishers are the best type to use on Class A fires. Water has two effects on fire. It deprives fire of oxygen and cools the material being burned.

notes.front: Why are water extinguishers not recommended for Class B fires?
notes.back: Most petroleum products float on water.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives this as its reason for not recommending water on burning liquids.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Since most petroleum products float on water, water-type fire extinguishers are not recommended for Class B fires.

notes.front: Why must a water extinguisher never be used on a Class D fire?
notes.back: Water’s cooling effect causes an explosive expansion of the metal.
notes.explanation: The handbook links this to metals burning at extremely high temperatures.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Never use water-type fire extinguishers on Class D fires. The cooling effect of water causes an explosive expansion of the metal, because metals burn at extremely high temperatures.

notes.front: On which classes of fire are CO2 extinguishers used?
notes.back: Class A, B and C.
notes.explanation: It puts the fire out by depriving it of oxygen.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguishers are used for Class A, B, and C fires, extinguishing the fire by depriving it of oxygen.

notes.front: On which classes of fire are halogenated hydrocarbon extinguishers most effective?
notes.back: Class B and C.
notes.explanation: They can be used on Class A and D fires, but the handbook says they are less effective there.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: Halogenated hydrocarbon extinguishers are most effective on Class B and C fires. They can be used on Class A and D fires, but they are less effective.

notes.front: Which type of extinguisher is best for Class D fires?
notes.back: Dry powder.
notes.explanation: Dry powder is also effective on Class B and C fires.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: Dry powder extinguishers, while effective on Class B and C fires, are best for use on Class D fires.

notes.front: When using a fire extinguisher, how far back should you stand and where should you aim?
notes.back: Stand back 8 feet and aim at the base of the fire or flames.
notes.explanation: Then squeeze the lever and sweep from side to side until the fire is out.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Using Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Stand back 8 feet and aim at the base of the fire or flames. Squeeze the lever and sweep side to side until the fire is extinguished.

notes.front: Spilled fuel is burning on the ramp. Which extinguisher type does the handbook advise against for this fire?
notes.choices:
A) Carbon dioxide
B) Water
C) Dry powder
D) Halon 1211
notes.back: B) Water
notes.choicesExplained: A: CO2 is used on Class A, B and C fires, so the handbook does not advise against it here. D: halogenated hydrocarbons are most effective on Class B and C fires. C: dry powder is effective on Class B and C fires.
notes.explanation: Burning fuel is a Class B fire, and the handbook does not recommend water there because most petroleum products float on water.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-5
notes.evidence: Since most petroleum products float on water, water-type fire extinguishers are not recommended for Class B fires.

notes.front: A magnesium part is burning in the shop. Which extinguisher does the handbook call best for this fire?
notes.choices:
A) Water
B) Carbon dioxide
C) Dry powder
D) Soda-acid
notes.back: C) Dry powder
notes.choicesExplained: A: water on burning metal can cause explosive expansion. B: CO2 must never be used on Class D fires. D: soda-acid is a water extinguisher, with the same danger as A.
notes.explanation: Burning magnesium is a Class D fire, and dry powder is the handbook’s best choice for Class D.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types and Operation of Shop and Flight Line Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: Dry powder extinguishers, while effective on Class B and C fires, are best for use on Class D fires.

notes.front: What are two condition checks on a fire extinguisher from the handbook’s minimum list?
notes.back: Any two of: gauge or indicator in operable range; proper weight; no nozzle obstruction; no obvious damage.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to use a checklist, and to check at least its minimum items when no checklist is available.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Inspection of Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-7
notes.evidence: • Gauge or indicator in operable range • Proper weight • No nozzle obstruction • No obvious damage

notes.front: On a periodic check with no checklist to hand, an extinguisher’s gauge reads in range, but its safety seal is broken. What should the inspector conclude?
notes.choices:
A) It passes, because the gauge is in range
B) It passes, because seals are only checked when a checklist exists
C) It passes if it is at least 3 feet from a wall marking
D) It fails a minimum check: safety seals must be unbroken
notes.back: D) It fails a minimum check: safety seals must be unbroken
notes.choicesExplained: A: the gauge is only one of the minimum items. B: the minimum list applies exactly when no checklist is available. C: the 3-foot figure is about how legible markings on the extinguisher must be.
notes.explanation: Unbroken safety seals are on the handbook’s minimum list, so a gauge in range alone does not pass the check.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Inspection of Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-7
notes.evidence: Fire extinguishers need to be checked periodically utilizing a checklist. If a checklist is unavailable, check the following as a minimum: Safety seals unbroken

notes.front: From what distance must extinguisher markings be identifiable, on the extinguisher and on nearby wall panels?
notes.back: At least 3 feet on the extinguisher; at least 25 feet on wall panels nearby.
notes.explanation: In each case the test is a person with average eyesight seeing and identifying the marking.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Identifying Fire Extinguishers”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: at a distance of at least 3 feet. When markings are applied to wall panels, and so forth, in the vicinity of extinguishers, they must be large enough and in a form that is easily seen and identifiable by the average person with average eyesight at a distance of at least 25 feet.

notes.front: When are aircraft to be tied down, and why?
notes.back: After each flight, to prevent damage from sudden storms.
notes.explanation: The direction in which they are parked and tied down is set by the prevailing or forecast wind.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Preparation of Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Aircraft are to be tied down after each flight to prevent damage from sudden storms. The direction that aircraft are to be parked and tied down is determined by prevailing or forecast wind direction.

notes.front: If tie-down reels are not available, what may be used instead?
notes.back: ¼" wire cable or 1½" manila line.
notes.explanation: Reels are normally attached to the aircraft’s tie-down loops and to anchors or stakes.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Preparation of Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Attach tie-down reels to aircraft tie-down loops, tiedown anchors, or tie-down stakes. Use tie-down stakes for temporary tie-down only. If tie-down reels are not available, 1⁄4" wire cable or 11⁄2" manila line may be used.

notes.front: An aircraft is to be parked outside for a month. The crew plan to secure it with tie-down stakes driven into the grass. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) Stakes are acceptable for any period
B) Stakes are for temporary tie-down only
C) Stakes are required whenever reels are unavailable
D) Stakes are only for seaplanes
notes.back: B) Stakes are for temporary tie-down only
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook limits stakes to temporary use. C: without reels, the alternative is ¼" wire cable or 1½" manila line, not stakes. D: stakes are listed among land-plane anchor points.
notes.explanation: The handbook limits tie-down stakes to temporary tie-down, so a month’s parking calls for proper anchors.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Preparation of Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Attach tie-down reels to aircraft tie-down loops, tiedown anchors, or tie-down stakes. Use tie-down stakes for temporary tie-down only.

notes.front: Why must a tie-down rope never be tied to a lift strut?
notes.back: It can bend the strut if the rope slips to a point where there is no slack.
notes.explanation: Light aircraft are most often secured with ropes tied only at the tie-down rings provided.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Securing Light Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Light aircraft are most often secured with ropes tied only at the aircraft tie-down rings provided for securing purposes. Rope is never to be tied to a lift strut, since this practice can bend a strut if the rope slips to a point where there is no slack.

notes.front: About how much slack should a manila tie-down rope have, and why?
notes.back: About 1 inch, because manila rope shrinks when wet.
notes.explanation: Too much slack, however, lets the aircraft jerk against the ropes.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Securing Light Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Since manila rope shrinks when wet, about 1 inch (1") of slack needs to be provided for movement. Too much slack, however, allows the aircraft to jerk against the ropes.

notes.front: To stop any movement, a mechanic hauls a light aircraft’s tie-down ropes drum-tight. What problem does the handbook describe?
notes.choices:
A) The ropes will shrink and slip off the rings
B) The ropes put inverted flight stresses on the aircraft
C) The knots cannot be untied
D) The aircraft will jerk against the ropes
notes.back: B) The ropes put inverted flight stresses on the aircraft
notes.choicesExplained: A: shrinking is the reason to leave slack, not an effect of tightness. D: jerking comes from too much slack. C: the handbook recommends anti-slip knots such as the bowline, which are easy to untie.
notes.explanation: Tight ropes put inverted flight stresses on the aircraft, which many are not designed to take.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Securing Light Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Tight tie-down ropes put inverted flight stresses on the aircraft and many are not designed to take such loads. A tie-down rope holds no better than the knot.

notes.front: What governs the number of tie-downs used on a heavy aircraft?
notes.back: The anticipated weather conditions.
notes.explanation: Heavy aircraft can be tied down with rope or cable.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Securing Heavy Aircraft”, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: The normal tie-down procedure for heavy aircraft can be accomplished with rope or cable tie-down. The number of tie-downs are governed by anticipated weather conditions.

notes.front: In securing a ski plane on ice or snow, what is a dead-man?
notes.back: Any item at hand, such as a pipe or log, tied to a rope and buried in a snow or ice trench.
notes.explanation: The free end of the rope is kept dry and unfrozen so that the aircraft can be tied to it.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Tie-Down Procedures for Ski Planes”, p. 1-9
notes.evidence: A dead-man is any item at hand, such as a piece of pipe, log, and so forth, that a rope is attached to and buried in a snow or ice trench. Using caution to keep the free end of the rope dry and unfrozen, snow is packed in the trench.

notes.front: Up to about what wind speed can a tied-down helicopter usually withstand?
notes.back: Approximately 65 mph.
notes.explanation: Helicopters are secured in hangars when possible, and tied down securely if not.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Tie-Down Procedures for Helicopters”, p. 1-10
notes.evidence: Helicopters are to be secured in hangars, when possible. If not, they must be tied down securely. Helicopters that are tied down can usually sustain winds up to approximately 65 mph.

notes.front: In high winds, how can the wing of a weight-shift-control aircraft be secured?
notes.back: Disconnect the mast from the wing, place the wing close to the ground and secure it.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls these aircraft very susceptible to wind damage.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Procedures for Securing Weight-Shift-Control”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: These types of aircraft are very susceptible to wind damage. The wings can be secured in a similar manner as a conventional aircraft in light winds. In high winds, the mast can be disconnected from the wing and the wing placed close to the ground and secured.

notes.front: Before starting an aircraft engine, why head the aircraft into the prevailing wind?
notes.back: To ensure adequate airflow over the engine for cooling.
notes.explanation: It is step 1 of the handbook’s list of things to do before starting an aircraft engine.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Engine Starting and Operation”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: 1. Position the aircraft to head into the prevailing wind to ensure adequate airflow over the engine for cooling purposes.

notes.front: Before starting a radial engine that has been shut down for more than 30 minutes, how is a hydraulic lock detected?
notes.back: Turn the propeller three or four complete revolutions by hand.
notes.explanation: Liquid in a cylinder shows as abnormal effort to turn the propeller, or the propeller stopping abruptly.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 1-12
notes.evidence: Turn the propeller three or four complete revolutions by hand to detect a hydraulic lock, if one is present. Any liquid present in a cylinder is indicated by the abnormal effort required to rotate the propeller or by the propeller stopping abruptly during rotation.

notes.front: For a typical reciprocating engine start, the throttle is opened to a position giving {{c1::1,000 to 1,200}} rpm.
notes.explanation: The handbook puts that at approximately ⅛" to ½" from the closed position.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: 3. Open the throttle to a position that provides 1,000 to 1,200 rpm (approximately 1⁄8" to 1⁄2" from the “closed” position).

notes.front: What starter duty cycle does the handbook give for starting a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: Crank for no more than 1 minute continuously, then allow 3 to 5 minutes for the starter to cool.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the starter may burn out from overheating.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: Do not crank the engine continuously with the starter for more than 1 minute. Allow a 3- to 5-minute period for cooling the starter (starter duty cycle) between successive attempts. Otherwise, the starter may be burned out due to overheating.

notes.front: If oil pressure does not show within {{c1::30 seconds}} of a reciprocating engine starting, stop the engine and find the trouble.
notes.explanation: If oil pressure does show, the throttle is set to the manufacturer’s warm-up rpm, usually 1,000 to 1,300 rpm.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: If oil pressure does not show within 30 seconds, stop the engine and determine the trouble. If oil pressure is indicated, adjust the throttle to the aircraft manufacturer’s specified rpm for engine warm up. Warm up rpm is usually between 1,000 to 1,300 rpm.

notes.front: Pulling a radial engine’s propeller through by hand before a start, a mechanic feels abnormal resistance, and the propeller stops abruptly. What is the correct next step?
notes.choices:
A) Apply more force until the propeller turns
B) Start the engine with the starter to clear the liquid
C) Pull the propeller through in the direction opposite to normal rotation
D) Remove the front or rear spark plug from the lower cylinders and pull the propeller through
notes.back: D) Remove the front or rear spark plug from the lower cylinders and pull the propeller through
notes.choicesExplained: A: force can bend or break a connecting rod when a lock is present. C: reverse rotation pushes the liquid into the intake pipe, from where it can lock the next start. B: the handbook’s method is removing a plug, not starting against the lock.
notes.explanation: This is a hydraulic lock; the handbook clears it by removing a spark plug from the lower cylinders and pulling the propeller through.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 1-12
notes.evidence: To eliminate a lock, remove either the front or rear spark plug from the lower cylinders and pull the propeller through. Never attempt to clear the hydraulic lock by pulling the propeller through in the direction opposite to normal rotation.

notes.front: During engine starting, what extinguisher should the fireguard have?
notes.back: A CO2 extinguisher of at least 5-pound capacity.
notes.explanation: The fireguard stands beside the outboard side of the engine, in view of the pilot, where starting problems can be seen.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Engine Starting and Operation”, p. 1-11
notes.evidence: The fire extinguisher should be a CO2 extinguisher of at least 5-pound capacity. The appropriate place is adjacent to the outboard side of the engine, in view of the pilot, and also where they can observe the engine/ aircraft for indication of starting problems.

notes.front: In an engine fire during starting, where does the fireguard direct the CO2?
notes.back: Into the engine’s air intake.
notes.explanation: That is why the handbook says the fireguard must know the engine’s induction system.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Extinguishing Engine Fires”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: The fireguard must be familiar with the induction system of the engine so that in case of fire, they can direct the CO2 into the air intake of the engine to extinguish it.

notes.front: During a reciprocating engine start, flames appear at the intake before the engine has fired. What should the operator do first?
notes.choices:
A) Stop cranking at once and leave the aircraft
B) Open the cowling to let the fire burn out
C) Switch the carburettor heat to hot
D) Continue cranking to start the engine and extinguish the fire
notes.back: D) Continue cranking to start the engine and extinguish the fire
notes.choicesExplained: A: stopping at once is the step only if the engine will not start and the fire keeps burning. B: the handbook gives no such step. C: carburettor heat is left in cold for starting, to prevent damage and fire in case of backfire.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to keep cranking to start the engine and put out the fire; only if it does not start and the fire keeps burning is the start abandoned.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Extinguishing Engine Fires”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: If an engine fire develops during the starting procedure, the operator should continue cranking to start the engine and extinguish the fire. If the engine does not start and the fire continues to burn, discontinue the start attempt.

notes.front: When hand propping, what does the person turning the propeller call first?
notes.back: “Fuel on, switch off, throttle closed, brakes on.”
notes.explanation: The person operating the engine checks those items and repeats the phrase.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hand Cranking Engines”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The person who is turning the propeller calls: “Fuel on, switch off, throttle closed, brakes on.” The person operating the engine checks these items and repeats the phrase.

notes.front: When hand propping, when may the operator turn the ignition switch on?
notes.back: Only after the person swinging the propeller calls “contact” and the operator repeats it.
notes.explanation: The switch and throttle are not touched again after the first call until “contact” is called.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hand Cranking Engines”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The switch and throttle must not be touched again until the person swinging the prop calls “contact.” The operator repeats “contact” and then turns on the switch. Never turn on the switch and then call “contact.”

notes.front: Why should you always assume the ignition is on when touching a propeller?
notes.back: A faulty magneto switch can read “off” yet still let current flow in the primary circuit, so the engine could start.
notes.explanation: Magneto switches turn the ignition off by short-circuiting the current, so a fault leaves the ignition live.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hand Cranking Engines”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: While touching a propeller, always assume that the ignition is on. The switches that control the magnetos operate on the principle of short-circuiting the current to turn the ignition off. If the switch is faulty, it can be in the “off” position and still permit current to flow in the magneto primary circuit.

notes.front: Before the helper at the propeller has said anything, the pilot switches on the ignition and then calls “contact”. What has gone wrong?
notes.choices:
A) The switch was turned on before the helper called “contact”
B) The pilot should have called “switch off” instead
C) The throttle should have been fully open
D) Nothing, provided the brakes are on
notes.back: A) The switch was turned on before the helper called “contact”
notes.choicesExplained: D: brakes do not make a live ignition safe. B: “switch off” belongs to the first call made by the person at the propeller. C: the first call specifies throttle closed.
notes.explanation: The handbook reverses this order: the person at the propeller calls “contact”, the operator repeats it, and only then switches on.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hand Cranking Engines”, p. 1-13
notes.evidence: The switch and throttle must not be touched again until the person swinging the prop calls “contact.” The operator repeats “contact” and then turns on the switch. Never turn on the switch and then call “contact.”

notes.front: What are the three steps of starting any turbine engine, in order?
notes.back: Starter turns the compressor for airflow; igniters on and fuel engaged; starter disengaged at self-sustaining speed.
notes.explanation: The igniters come on only once the compressor is turning fast enough to give enough airflow.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Turboprop Engines”, p. 1-14
notes.evidence: The starter turns the main compressor to provide airflow though the engine. At the correct speed that provides enough airflow, the igniters are turned on and provide a hot spark to light the fuel that is engaged next. As the engine accelerates, it reaches a selfsustaining speed and the starter is disengaged.

notes.front: Does a turbine-powered aircraft need a preflight run-up?
notes.back: No, unless one is needed to investigate a suspected malfunction.
notes.explanation: The handbook contrasts this with reciprocating-engine aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Turbofan Engines”, p. 1-15
notes.evidence: Unlike reciprocating engine aircraft, the turbine-powered aircraft does not require a preflight run-up unless it is necessary to investigate a suspected malfunction.

notes.front: In a turbofan start, what indicates light-off?
notes.back: A rise in exhaust gas temperature.
notes.explanation: On a two-spool engine the next check is rotation of the fan.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Starting a Turbofan Engine”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: 7. Engine start (light off) is indicated by a rise in exhaust gas temperature. 8. If a two-spool engine, check rotation of fan or N1.

notes.front: In a turbofan start, the fuel has been turned on but exhaust gas temperature has not risen by the end of the predetermined time. What should happen?
notes.choices:
A) Discontinue the start, as a malfunction is indicated
B) Keep the fuel on and wait for light-off
C) Add more fuel to force light-off
D) Disengage the starter and let the engine accelerate
notes.back: A) Discontinue the start, as a malfunction is indicated
notes.choicesExplained: B: waiting beyond the set time is what the handbook rules out. C: extra fuel is not a handbook remedy, and too much fuel causes hot starts. D: the starter is disengaged only once the engine is self-sustaining.
notes.explanation: The handbook says exceeding that interval indicates a malfunction and the start must be discontinued.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Starting a Turbofan Engine”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: the engine “lights off” within a predetermined time after the fuel is turned on. This time interval, if exceeded, indicates a malfunction has occurred and the start must be discontinued.

notes.front: At what rpm does an APU idle with no load?
notes.back: 100 percent rpm.
notes.explanation: During its start the exhaust gas temperature must be monitored.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Auxiliary Power Units (APUs)”, p. 1-16
notes.evidence: During start, the exhaust gas temperature must be monitored. APUs are at idle at 100 percent rpm with no load.

notes.front: What can cause the rich mixture behind a hot start, and what must be done at once?
notes.back: Too much fuel or not enough airflow; shut off the fuel to the engine immediately.
notes.explanation: The handbook traces a hot start to an excessively rich air-fuel mixture in the combustion chamber.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hot Start”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: This is usually caused by an excessively rich air-fuel mixture entering the combustion chamber. This condition can be caused by either too much fuel or not enough airflow. The fuel to the engine must be shut off immediately.

notes.front: What often causes a hung start?
notes.back: Insufficient power to the starter, or the starter cutting off before the engine starts self-accelerating.
notes.explanation: Either way the rpm stays low, and the handbook says to shut the engine down.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “False or Hung Start”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: This is often the result of insufficient power to the starter or the starter cutting off before the engine starts self-accelerating. In this case, shut the engine down.

notes.front: After any unsatisfactory turbine start, how is accumulated fuel cleared?
notes.back: Fuel and ignition off, then rotate the compressor for about 15 seconds; if it cannot be motored, allow a 30-second draining period.
notes.explanation: The handbook applies this to all cases of unsatisfactory starts, before another start is attempted.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Engine Fails to Start”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: In all cases of unsatisfactory starts, the fuel and ignition must be turned off. Continue rotating the compressor for approximately 15 seconds to remove accumulated fuel from the engine. If unable to motor (rotate) the engine, allow a 30-second fuel draining period before attempting another start.

notes.front: During a turbine start the engine lights off and accelerates, but exhaust gas temperature climbs past its limit. Which kind of unsatisfactory start is this?
notes.choices:
A) Hung start
B) Engine fails to start
C) Hot start
D) A normal start
notes.back: C) Hot start
notes.choicesExplained: A: in a hung start rpm stays low; the problem here is temperature. B: the engine has started. D: exceeding the temperature limit makes the start unsatisfactory.
notes.explanation: The engine has started but exhaust gas temperature exceeds specified limits, which is the handbook’s definition of a hot start.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Unsatisfactory Turbine Engine Starts”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: A hot start occurs when the engine starts, but the exhaust gas temperature exceeds specified limits.

notes.front: A turbine lights off normally, but rpm stays at a low value and will not rise to normal starting rpm; exhaust gas temperature is within limits. Which kind of start is this?
notes.choices:
A) Hung start
B) Hot start
C) Engine fails to start
D) Torching
notes.back: A) Hung start
notes.choicesExplained: B: exhaust gas temperature is within limits. C: the engine has lit off. D: torching is visible burning in the exhaust nozzle.
notes.explanation: A normal light-off followed by rpm stuck at a low value is the handbook’s false or hung start.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Unsatisfactory Turbine Engine Starts”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: False or hung starts occur when the engine starts normally, but the rpm remains at some low value rather than increasing to the normal starting rpm.

notes.front: The starter turns a turbine and fuel is on, but the engine has not started when the prescribed time runs out. The ignition exciter is found to have no power. Which kind of start is this?
notes.choices:
A) Hot start
B) Engine fails to start
C) A normal start
D) Hung start
notes.back: B) Engine fails to start
notes.choicesExplained: A: a hot start needs the engine to have started. D: in a hung start the engine starts but rpm stays low. C: it did not start within the time limit.
notes.explanation: Failing to start within the prescribed time is the handbook’s “engine fails to start”, and no power to the exciter is one of its listed causes.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Unsatisfactory Turbine Engine Starts”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: The engine failing to start within the prescribed time limit can be caused by lack of fuel to the engine, insufficient or no electrical power to the exciter in the ignition system, or incorrect fuel mixture.

notes.front: Before an aircraft is towed, who must be in the flight deck, and why?
notes.back: A qualified person, to operate the brakes in case the tow bar fails or becomes unhooked.
notes.explanation: The aircraft can then be stopped before it is damaged.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: Before the aircraft to be towed is moved, a qualified person must be in the flight deck to operate the brakes in case the tow bar fails or becomes unhooked. The aircraft can then be stopped, preventing possible damage.

notes.front: Whenever a tail-wheel aircraft is towed, what must be done with the tail wheel?
notes.back: It must be unlocked.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the tail wheel locking mechanism may be damaged or break.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: Any time an aircraft equipped with a tail wheel is towed, the tail wheel must be unlocked or the tail wheel locking mechanism may damage or break.

notes.front: On an aircraft with a steerable nosewheel, how are the locking scissors set for towing?
notes.back: To full swivel, and reset after the tow bar has been removed.
notes.explanation: People in the aircraft must not try to steer the nosewheel while the tow bar is attached.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: the locking scissors are set to full swivel for towing. The locking device must be reset after the tow bar has been removed from the aircraft. Persons stationed in the aircraft are not to attempt to steer or turn the nosewheel when the tow bar is attached to the aircraft.

notes.front: What is the limit on towing speed?
notes.back: It must not exceed the speed of the walking team members.
notes.explanation: The same list forbids boarding or leaving a moving aircraft or towing vehicle.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: In the interest of safety, no attempt to board or leave a moving aircraft or towing vehicle is permitted. The towing speed of the aircraft is not to exceed that of the walking team members.

notes.front: Halfway through a tow, a team member steps between the nosewheel and the tug to check the tow-bar pin while the aircraft is moving. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) It is allowed if the tow speed is below walking pace
B) No one may walk or ride between the nosewheel and the towing vehicle
C) It is allowed if a wing walker is watching
D) It is allowed if the aircraft brakes are applied
notes.back: B) No one may walk or ride between the nosewheel and the towing vehicle
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule has no speed exception. C: wing walkers check wingtip clearance; they do not make this allowed. D: aircraft brakes must never be applied during towing except on a team member’s emergency command.
notes.explanation: The handbook says no one may walk or ride between the nosewheel and the towing vehicle under any circumstances.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: Under no circumstances is anyone permitted to walk or to ride between the nosewheel of an aircraft and the towing vehicle, nor ride on the outside of a moving aircraft or on the towing vehicle.

notes.front: Before any movement of an aircraft across runways or taxiways, what must be done?
notes.back: Contact the airport control tower on the appropriate frequency for clearance to proceed.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists this among its typical towing and parking procedures.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: 14. Prior to any movement of aircraft across runways or taxiways, contact the airport control tower on the appropriate frequency for clearance to proceed.

notes.front: A tow team must cross an active taxiway to reach the maintenance hangar. The taxiway looks empty. What must they do first?
notes.choices:
A) Cross quickly while the taxiway is empty
B) Wait for a flashing white light from the tower
C) Post a wing walker at the taxiway edge and cross
D) Contact the control tower on the appropriate frequency for clearance
notes.back: D) Contact the control tower on the appropriate frequency for clearance
notes.choicesExplained: A: an empty-looking taxiway is not clearance. C: wing walkers check clearance from obstructions, not runway traffic. B: flashing white means return to starting point.
notes.explanation: The handbook requires tower clearance before moving any aircraft across runways or taxiways, whatever the traffic looks like.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Towing of Aircraft”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: 14. Prior to any movement of aircraft across runways or taxiways, contact the airport control tower on the appropriate frequency for clearance to proceed.

notes.front: An aircraft must be moved under its own power to the run-up area. As a general rule, who is authorised to start and taxi it?
notes.choices:
A) Any member of the tow team
B) The fuel truck driver
C) A rated pilot or a qualified A&P technician
D) Whoever holds the aircraft keys
notes.back: C) A rated pilot or a qualified A&P technician
notes.choicesExplained: A: tow teams move aircraft by tug, not under power. B: fuellers are not in the handbook’s rule. D: holding the keys confers no authority in the handbook.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s general rule limits starting, run-up and taxiing to rated pilots and qualified airframe and powerplant (A&P) technicians.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Taxiing Aircraft”, p. 1-19
notes.evidence: As a general rule, only rated pilots and qualified airframe and powerplant (A&P) technicians are authorized to start, run up, and taxi aircraft.

notes.front: What is the standard position for a taxi signalman?
notes.back: Slightly ahead of and in line with the aircraft’s left wingtip.
notes.explanation: Facing the aircraft from there, the signalman has the aircraft’s nose on the left.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Taxi Signals”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: The standard position for a signalman is slightly ahead of and in line with the aircraft’s left wingtip. As the signalman faces the aircraft, the nose of the aircraft is on the left.

image.alt: Plan view of an aircraft with its nose pointing up the page. A marker for the taxi signalman stands slightly ahead of the left wingtip and in line with it; a dashed arrow shows the signalman facing the aircraft, with the nose to the signalman’s left.
