notes.front: What simple test tells a taxi signalman that the pilot can see the signals?
notes.back: If the signalman can see the pilot’s eyes, the pilot can see the signals.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it a foolproof test and good practice.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Taxi Signals”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: It is a good practice to perform a foolproof test to be sure the pilot can see all signals. If the signalman can see the pilot’s eyes, the pilot can see the signals.

notes.front: How is the stop signal given at night?
notes.back: As the emergency stop: wands crossed to form a lighted “X” above and in front of the head.
notes.explanation: Other night signals are made the same way as day signals, using illuminated wands.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Taxi Signals”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: Night signals are made in the same manner as day signals with the exception of the stop signal. The stop signal used at night is the “emergence stop” signal. This signal is made by crossing the wands to form a lighted “X” above and in front of the head.

notes.front: A signalman is guiding an aircraft into a stand, but the pilot does not seem to be following the signals. What should the signalman do?
notes.choices:
A) Walk closer to the nose so the pilot can hear
B) Repeat the last signal faster
C) Hand over to a wing walker
D) Give the “stop” sign and begin the series of signals again
notes.back: D) Give the “stop” sign and begin the series of signals again
notes.choicesExplained: A: walking in front of the aircraft abandons the standard position, and the handbook’s answer is the stop sign. B: faster signals risk the indistinct signals the handbook warns against. C: the handbook gives no hand-over step.
notes.explanation: The handbook says that with any doubt, or a pilot not following, the signalman gives “stop” and starts the series again.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Taxi Signals”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: If there is any doubt about a signal, or if the pilot does not appear to be following the signals, use the “stop” sign and begin the series of signals again.

notes.front: In the standard taxi light signals, what does a flashing green light mean?
notes.back: Cleared to taxi.
notes.explanation: Steady red, by contrast, means stop.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-22. Standard taxi light signals”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Lights Meaning Flashing green Cleared to taxi Steady red Stop Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use Flashing white Return to starting point Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution

notes.front: In the standard taxi light signals, what does a steady red light mean?
notes.back: Stop.
notes.explanation: A flashing red light, by contrast, means taxi clear of the runway in use.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-22. Standard taxi light signals”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Lights Meaning Flashing green Cleared to taxi Steady red Stop Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use Flashing white Return to starting point Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution

notes.front: In the standard taxi light signals, what does a flashing red light mean?
notes.back: Taxi clear of the runway in use.
notes.explanation: A steady red light, by contrast, means stop.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-22. Standard taxi light signals”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Lights Meaning Flashing green Cleared to taxi Steady red Stop Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use Flashing white Return to starting point Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution

notes.front: In the standard taxi light signals, what does a flashing white light mean?
notes.back: Return to starting point.
notes.explanation: It is the only white signal in the set of five.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-22. Standard taxi light signals”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Lights Meaning Flashing green Cleared to taxi Steady red Stop Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use Flashing white Return to starting point Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution

notes.front: In the standard taxi light signals, what does alternating red and green mean?
notes.back: Exercise extreme caution.
notes.explanation: It is the only signal in the set that mixes two colours.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-22. Standard taxi light signals”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Lights Meaning Flashing green Cleared to taxi Steady red Stop Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use Flashing white Return to starting point Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution

notes.front: A mechanic taxiing an aircraft on a runway sees a flashing red light from the tower. What should they do?
notes.choices:
A) Taxi clear of the runway in use
B) Stop where they are and wait
C) Return to the starting point
D) Continue, as they are cleared to taxi
notes.back: A) Taxi clear of the runway in use
notes.choicesExplained: B: stop is steady red. C: return to starting point is flashing white. D: cleared to taxi is flashing green.
notes.explanation: In the standard taxi light signals, flashing red means taxi clear of the runway in use.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-22. Standard taxi light signals”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Lights Meaning Flashing green Cleared to taxi Steady red Stop Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use Flashing white Return to starting point Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution

notes.front: When is engine oil checked on a reciprocating engine, and when on a turbine engine?
notes.back: Reciprocating: after the engine has been inactive. Turbine: just after shutdown.
notes.explanation: In both cases oil is checked with a dipstick or sight gauge marked for the correct level.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Servicing Aircraft Air/Nitrogen Oil & Fluids”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: In general, aircraft engine oil is checked with a dipstick or a sight gauge. There are markings on the stick or around the sight gauge to determine the correct level. Reciprocating engines are to be checked after the engine has been inactive, while the turbine engine must be checked just after shutdown.

notes.front: Why can a dry sump engine be overfilled if it is serviced too soon?
notes.back: Oil seeps from the tank into the gearcase and does not show on the dipstick until the engine is started or motored.
notes.explanation: If oil is added before that oil is pumped back to the tank, the engine ends up overfilled.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Servicing Aircraft Air/Nitrogen Oil & Fluids”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: Dry sump oil systems tend to hide oil that has seeped from the oil tank into the gearcase of the engine. This oil does not show up on the dipstick until the engine has been started or motored. If serviced before this oil is pumped back into the tank, the engine overfills.

notes.front: Why must an oil tank never be overfilled?
notes.back: Oil foams as it circulates through the engine, and the tank’s expansion space allows for this foaming.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes the foaming as oil mixing with air.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Servicing Aircraft Air/Nitrogen Oil & Fluids”, p. 1-20
notes.evidence: Never overfill the oil tank. Oil foams as it is circulated through the engine. The expansion space in the oil tank allows for this foaming (oil mixing with air).

notes.front: A technician is about to change a hydraulic filter on an aircraft whose system was pressurised a few minutes ago. What must be ensured first?
notes.choices:
A) That a hydraulic ground power unit is running
B) That the reservoir is overfilled to allow for loss
C) That the pressure is off the system
D) That the fluid colour matches the jet fuel band
notes.back: C) That the pressure is off the system
notes.choicesExplained: B: overfilling is not a handbook step, and the need is to relieve pressure. A: a running power unit would pressurise the system. D: fuel colour bands have nothing to do with hydraulic fluid.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to make sure the pressure is off the system before removing filters, and to purge air and leak-check afterwards if much fluid was lost.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Servicing Aircraft Air/Nitrogen Oil & Fluids”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Also, if changing hydraulic filters, assure that the pressure is off the system before removing the filters. After servicing the filters (if large amounts of fluids were lost) or system quantity, air must be purged and the system checked for leaks.

notes.front: Larger generator power units supply what kind of DC for starting turbine engines, and for reciprocating engines?
notes.back: Constant-current, variable-voltage DC for turbine engines; constant-voltage DC for reciprocating engines.
notes.explanation: These are the larger towed units equipped with generators, which give a wider range of output power.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Electric Ground Power Units”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Larger units are equipped with generators. Providing a wider range of output power, these power units are normally designed to supply constant-current, variable voltage DC electrical power for starting turbine aircraft engines and constant-voltage DC for starting reciprocating aircraft engines.

notes.front: When must a ground power unit never be moved?
notes.back: When service cables are attached to an aircraft or the generator system is engaged.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that all electrical safety precautions apply when servicing an aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Electric Ground Power Units”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: Observe all electrical safety precautions when servicing an aircraft. Additionally, never move a power unit when service cables are attached to an aircraft or when the generator system is engaged.

notes.front: A GPU is being parked to power an aircraft. The operator puts it right under the wing with the cable coiled, to keep the cable short. What does the handbook require instead?
notes.choices:
A) A position under the nose instead of the wing
B) The cable stretched tight so it cannot be tripped over
C) A position clear of collision if its brakes fail, cable near full length
D) Nothing, provided the generator is switched off
notes.back: C) A position clear of collision if its brakes fail, cable near full length
notes.choicesExplained: A: under the nose is still too close for a unit whose brakes might fail. B: the handbook warns against stretching the cable or stressing the aircraft receptacle. D: the positioning rule applies while the unit supplies power.
notes.explanation: The handbook asks for a position that avoids a collision if the unit’s brakes fail, with the cable extended to near full length but not stretched.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Electric Ground Power Units”, p. 1-21
notes.evidence: When using ground electrical power units, it is important to position the unit to prevent collision with the aircraft being serviced, or others nearby, in the event the brakes on the unit fail. It must be parked so that the service cable is extended to near its full length away from the aircraft being serviced

notes.front: Why is extreme caution needed around a hydraulic power unit at 3,000 psi?
notes.back: At 3,000 psi a small stream from a leak can cut like a sharp knife.
notes.explanation: So the handbook asks for lines to be inspected for cuts and frays and kept free of kinks and twists.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Hydraulic Ground Power Units”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: At 3,000 psi, a small stream from a leak can cut like a sharp knife. Therefore, inspect lines used with the system for cuts, frays, or any other damage, and keep them free of kinks and twists.

notes.front: Where does the air from an air cart come from?
notes.back: Bleed air from the compressor of an APU built into the cart.
notes.explanation: The air is used for operating aircraft systems or starting engines.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Ground Support Air Units”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: built into the cart that provides bleed air from the APU’s compressor for operating aircraft systems or starting engines.

notes.front: How many people are required to service an aircraft with gaseous oxygen, and where are they stationed?
notes.back: Two: one at the servicing equipment’s control valves, one where the aircraft system pressure can be seen.
notes.explanation: The handbook requires the two to communicate in case of an emergency.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Oxygen Servicing Equipment”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: Two personnel are required to service an aircraft with gaseous oxygen. One person is stationed at the control valves of the servicing equipment, and one person is stationed where they can observe the pressure in the aircraft system. Communication between the two people is required in the event of an emergency.

notes.front: Which oxygen may be used in aircraft breathing oxygen systems?
notes.back: Only oxygen marked “Aviator’s Breathing Oxygen” meeting Federal Specification `BB-0-925A`, Grade A, or its equivalent.
notes.explanation: Oxygen is sold as aviator’s breathing, industrial and medical, and only the first qualifies.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Oxygen Servicing Equipment”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: Oxygen is commercially available in three general types: aviator’s breathing, industrial, and medical. Only oxygen marked “Aviator’s Breathing Oxygen” that meets Federal Specification BB-0-925A, Grade A, or its equivalent is to be used in aircraft breathing oxygen systems.

notes.front: The usual supply has run out, and a colleague offers a cylinder of medical oxygen, saying it is purer than anything else. Why does the handbook rule it out for aircraft breathing systems?
notes.choices:
A) It may contain impurities that make people sick
B) It is flammable
C) It contains water that can freeze at altitude
D) It is stored as liquid oxygen only
notes.back: C) It contains water that can freeze at altitude
notes.choicesExplained: A: impurities are the handbook’s objection to industrial oxygen. B: the handbook calls gaseous oxygen nonflammable. D: the handbook says nothing of the kind about medical oxygen.
notes.explanation: The handbook says medical oxygen, though pure, contains water that can freeze at the cold temperatures of altitudes where oxygen is needed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Oxygen Servicing Equipment”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: Industrial oxygen may contain impurities that could cause the pilot, crew, and/ or passengers to become sick. Medical oxygen, although pure, contains water that can freeze in the cold temperatures found at the altitudes where oxygen is necessary.

notes.front: What does oxygen form when it combines with oil, grease or bituminous material?
notes.back: A highly explosive mixture that is sensitive to compression or impact.
notes.explanation: The handbook also calls for the highest standard of cleanliness in handling oxygen.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Oxygen Hazards”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: In addition, oxygen combines with oil, grease, or bituminous material to form a highly-explosive mixture that is sensitive to compression or impact. Physical damage to, or failure of, oxygen containers, valves, or plumbing can result in an explosive rupture with extreme danger to life and property. It is imperative that the highest standard of cleanliness be observed in handling oxygen

notes.front: Is gaseous oxygen itself flammable?
notes.back: No. It is chemically stable and nonflammable, but combustibles ignite faster and burn more intensely in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
notes.explanation: The hazard is to everything around it: in an oxygen-rich atmosphere, combustible materials ignite more rapidly and burn with greater intensity.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Oxygen Hazards”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Gaseous oxygen is chemically stable and is nonflammable. However, combustible materials ignite more rapidly and burn with greater intensity in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

notes.front: About to connect an oxygen servicing hose, a technician notices a smear of grease on the aircraft’s filler fitting. What is the concern?
notes.choices:
A) Grease and oxygen can form a highly explosive mixture
B) The grease will freeze at altitude
C) Grease will contaminate the jet fuel
D) None: oxygen is nonflammable, so grease does not matter
notes.back: A) Grease and oxygen can form a highly explosive mixture
notes.choicesExplained: B: freezing at altitude is the handbook’s objection to the water in medical oxygen. C: the fitting is on the oxygen system, not the fuel system. D: oxygen itself does not burn, but it makes other materials ignite faster, and with grease it forms an explosive mixture.
notes.explanation: Oxygen and grease together form a highly explosive mixture that is sensitive to compression or impact.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Oxygen Hazards”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: In addition, oxygen combines with oil, grease, or bituminous material to form a highly-explosive mixture that is sensitive to compression or impact.

notes.front: What colour is grade 80 AVGAS?
notes.back: Red.
notes.explanation: Grade 80 is the lowest grade in the handbook’s colour reference.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Color Grade Red 80 Green 100 Blue 100LL Purple 115 Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference.

notes.front: What colour is grade 100 AVGAS?
notes.back: Green.
notes.explanation: Blue, by contrast, is grade 100LL.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Color Grade Red 80 Green 100 Blue 100LL Purple 115 Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference.

notes.front: What colour is grade 100LL AVGAS?
notes.back: Blue.
notes.explanation: Green, by contrast, is plain grade 100.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Color Grade Red 80 Green 100 Blue 100LL Purple 115 Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference.

notes.front: What colour is grade 115 AVGAS?
notes.back: Purple.
notes.explanation: It is the highest grade in the handbook’s colour reference.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Color Grade Red 80 Green 100 Blue 100LL Purple 115 Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference.

notes.front: What must the colour of AVGAS match?
notes.back: The colour band on the piping and fuelling equipment.
notes.explanation: The colour code is a second way to identify AVGAS, alongside its grade.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: AVGAS can also be identified by a color code. The color of the fuel needs to match the color band on piping and fueling equipment.

notes.front: A fuel sample drained from an aircraft’s sump is green. Which grade of AVGAS does the colour indicate?
notes.choicesExplained: A: grade 80 is red. D: 100LL is blue. C: 115 is purple.
notes.explanation: In the handbook’s colour reference, green is grade 100.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Color Grade Red 80 Green 100 Blue 100LL Purple 115 Figure 1-31. Aviation gasoline color and grade reference.

notes.front: Which three AVGAS grades does the handbook list as in general use?
notes.explanation: A fourth grade, 115/145, is in limited use in large reciprocating-engine aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Currently, there are three grades of fuel in general use: 80/87, 100/130, and 100LL (low lead). A fourth grade, 115/145, is in limited use in the large reciprocating-engine aircraft.

notes.front: In 80/87 AVGAS, what do the 80 and the 87 mean?
notes.back: 80 is the lean mixture octane rating; 87 is the rich mixture rating.
notes.explanation: To avoid confusion, AVGAS is generally identified by the first number alone, as grade 80, 100, 100LL or 115.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The two numbers indicate the lean mixture and rich mixture octane rating numbers of the specific fuel. In other words, with 80/87 AVGAS, the 80 is the lean mixture rating and 87 is the rich mixture rating number. To avoid confusing the types of AVGAS, it is generally identified as grade 80,

notes.front: An older document lists a fuel as 100/130 AVGAS. What is its rich mixture octane rating?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 100 is the lean mixture rating. C: the two numbers are separate ratings, not parts of a sum. D: 115 is a different grade.
notes.explanation: In a two-number grade, the first number is the lean mixture rating and the second is the rich mixture rating.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The two numbers indicate the lean mixture and rich mixture octane rating numbers of the specific fuel. In other words, with 80/87 AVGAS, the 80 is the lean mixture rating and 87 is the rich mixture rating number.

notes.front: Which three turbine fuels are generally used in civil aviation, and what are they made from?
notes.back: JET A and JET A-1, made from kerosene, and JET B, a blend of kerosene and AVGAS.
notes.explanation: Turbine fuel powers turbojet and turboshaft engines, while AVGAS is for reciprocating engines.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Turbine fuel/jet fuel is used to power turbojet and turboshaft engines. Three types of turbine fuel generally used in civilian aviation are JET A and JET A-1, made from kerosene, and JET B, a blend of kerosene and AVGAS.

notes.front: What are the effects of adding jet fuel to AVGAS, and of adding AVGAS to jet fuel?
notes.back: Jet fuel in AVGAS: less power and possible detonation damage and loss of life. AVGAS in jet fuel: lead deposits and reduced service life.
notes.explanation: The second harm is specific to turbine engines, where lead from the AVGAS deposits.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Adding jet fuel to AVGAS causes a decrease in the power developed by the engine and could cause damage to the engine (through detonation) and loss of life. Adding AVGAS to jet fuel can cause lead deposits in the turbine engine and can lead to reduced service life.

notes.front: What colour identifies jet fuel on piping and fuelling equipment, and what colour is the fuel itself?
notes.back: Black on piping and equipment; the fuel itself is clear or straw coloured.
notes.explanation: So the fuel’s own appearance will not match the black marking.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: While jet fuel is identified by the color black on piping and fueling equipment, the actual color of jet fuel can be clear or straw colored.

notes.front: A fueller is asked to fill a piston-engine trainer that takes 100LL. The hose they pick up has a black band. What does the band tell them?
notes.choices:
A) The hose carries 100LL
B) The hose carries grade 80
C) The band shows only that the hose is grounded
D) The hose carries jet fuel, the wrong fuel for this aircraft
notes.back: D) The hose carries jet fuel, the wrong fuel for this aircraft
notes.choicesExplained: A: 100LL is blue. B: grade 80 is red. C: the colour band identifies the fuel, not the grounding.
notes.explanation: Black on piping and fuelling equipment identifies jet fuel; 100LL would be blue.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: While jet fuel is identified by the color black on piping and fueling equipment, the actual color of jet fuel can be clear or straw colored.

notes.front: Before fuelling, what must the person fuelling ensure about the fuel itself?
notes.back: That the proper type and grade is used, and that AVGAS and JET fuel are not mixed.
notes.explanation: The next item on the same list is making sure all the sumps have been drained.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Procedures”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: 4. Ensure that the proper type and grade of fuel is used. Do not mix AVGAS and JET fuel. 5. Ensure that all the sumps have been drained.

notes.front: A piston single needs fuel and only a JET A truck is available. The pilot says a few gallons of jet fuel in the AVGAS will do no harm. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) Jet fuel in AVGAS reduces power and could cause detonation damage
B) Jet fuel in AVGAS only causes lead deposits
C) A small amount is harmless in any engine
D) Jet fuel raises the octane rating of AVGAS
notes.back: A) Jet fuel in AVGAS reduces power and could cause detonation damage
notes.choicesExplained: B: lead deposits come from AVGAS in jet fuel, in turbine engines. C: the handbook sets no harmless amount. D: the handbook says nothing of the kind; it warns of detonation.
notes.explanation: Jet fuel in AVGAS reduces engine power and could cause detonation damage and loss of life.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Types of Fuel and Identification”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Adding jet fuel to AVGAS causes a decrease in the power developed by the engine and could cause damage to the engine (through detonation) and loss of life.

notes.front: What types of contamination does the handbook list for aviation fuel?
notes.back: Water, solids and microbial growths.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls its control extremely important, since contamination can lead to engine failure or stoppage and loss of life.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Contamination Control”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The types of contamination found in aviation fuel include water, solids, and microbial growths. The control of contamination in aviation fuel is extremely important, since contamination can lead to engine failure or stoppage and the loss of life.

notes.front: When does dissolved water in fuel become a problem?
notes.back: When falling temperature turns it into free water, and ice crystals can form and clog filters and small orifices.
notes.explanation: Water in fuel generally takes two forms, dissolved (vapour) and free water.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Contamination Control”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Water in aviation fuels generally take two forms: dissolved (vapor) and free water. The dissolved water is not a major problem until, as the temperature lowers, it becomes free water. This then poses a problem if ice crystals form, clogging filters and other small orifices.

notes.front: How do water slugs differ from entrained water in fuel?
notes.back: Slugs are concentrations of water, drained after fuelling; entrained water is suspended droplets that make the fuel look cloudy.
notes.explanation: Both are forms of free water, and entrained water settles out in time.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Contamination Control”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Free water can appear as water slugs or entrained water. Water slugs are concentrations of water. This is the water that is drained after fueling an aircraft. Entrained water is suspended water droplets. These droplets may not be visible to the eye but give the fuel a cloudy look. The entrained water settles out in time.

notes.front: What does the handbook call the best way to prevent microbial growth in fuel?
notes.back: Keep the fuel dry.
notes.explanation: Warm temperatures and iron oxide and mineral salts in the water favour the growth.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Contamination Control”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Favorable conditions for the growth of micro-organisms in the fuel are warm temperatures and the presence of iron oxide and mineral salts in the water. The best way to prevent microbial growth is to keep the fuel dry.

notes.front: A freshly drawn jet fuel sample looks hazy and cloudy, but there is no separate layer of water at the bottom of the jar. Which contaminant does this best match?
notes.choices:
A) Entrained water
B) A water slug
C) Solid contamination
D) Lead deposits
notes.back: A) Entrained water
notes.choicesExplained: B: a slug is a concentration of water, the kind that is drained off. C: solids such as rust, sand or lint are insoluble particles. D: lead deposits form in turbine engines when AVGAS is added to jet fuel.
notes.explanation: Suspended water droplets that give the fuel a cloudy look are what the handbook calls entrained water.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Contamination Control”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Entrained water is suspended water droplets. These droplets may not be visible to the eye but give the fuel a cloudy look. The entrained water settles out in time.

notes.front: What is volatility, and which state of aviation fuel burns?
notes.back: The ability of a liquid to change into a gas at relatively low temperature; the vapour burns, not the liquid.
notes.explanation: The handbook says it is the vapour that both powers the aircraft and creates the fire hazard.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Hazards”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Volatility is the ability of a liquid to change into a gas at a relatively low temperature. In its liquid state, aviation fuel does not burn. It is, therefore, the vapor or gaseous state that the liquid fuel changes that is not only useful in powering the aircraft, but also a fire hazard.

notes.front: What is the greatest static electricity concern when fuelling an aircraft?
notes.back: Static built up in the airframe in flight trying to reach ground through the fuel line from the servicing unit.
notes.explanation: The handbook says this build-up must be dissipated before refuelling.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Hazards”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: The greatest static electricity concern around aircraft is that during flight, the aircraft moving through the air causes static electricity to build in the airframe. If that static electricity is not dissipated prior to refueling, the static electricity in the airframe attempts to return to the ground through the fuel line from the servicing unit.

notes.front: What are the two basic fuelling methods, and which aircraft use each?
notes.back: Over-the-wing for smaller aircraft; single point fuelling for larger aircraft.
notes.explanation: Single point fuelling uses receptacles in the bottom leading edge of the wing to fill all the tanks.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Procedures”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Smaller aircraft are fueled by the over-the-wing method. This method uses the fuel hose to fill through fueling ports on the top of the wing. The method used for larger aircraft is the single point fueling system. This type of fueling system uses receptacles in the bottom leading edge of the wing to fill all the tanks.

notes.front: When fuelling from a truck, in what order are the grounds connected?
notes.back: Ground the aircraft, then the truck, then bond the two together.
notes.explanation: This can be done with three separate ground wires or with a “Y” cable from the truck.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Procedures”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: 3. Ground the aircraft and then ground the truck. Next, ground or bond them together by running a connecting wire between the aircraft and the fuel truck. This may be done by three separate ground wires or by a “Y”

notes.front: In the fuelling sequence, ground the {{c1::nozzle}} to the aircraft, then open the fuel tank.
notes.explanation: It is step 5 of the handbook’s sequence for fuelling from mobile equipment.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Procedures”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: 5. Ground the nozzle to the aircraft, then open the fuel tank.

notes.front: Do not fuel an aircraft when there is lightning within {{c1::5 miles}}.
notes.explanation: The same list also forbids fuelling within 500 feet of operating ground radar.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Procedures”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: 8. Do not fuel an aircraft when there is lightning within 5 miles. 9. Do not fuel an aircraft within 500 feet of operating ground radar.

notes.front: A fueller clips the aircraft ground wire to the propeller because it is the nearest bare metal. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) The propeller must not be used; use bare metal or the proper grounding points
B) The propeller is acceptable because it is bare metal
C) The propeller is acceptable if the nozzle is grounded first
D) Grounding is only needed for single point fuelling
notes.back: A) The propeller must not be used; use bare metal or the proper grounding points
notes.choicesExplained: B: bare metal is required, but the handbook specifically excludes the propeller. C: grounding the nozzle does not make the propeller acceptable. D: the handbook’s grounding steps apply to fuelling from trucks, pits and cabinets alike.
notes.explanation: The handbook bars the exhaust and propeller as grounding points: the propeller can be damaged, and there is no quick way to ensure a positive engine-to-airframe bond.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Fueling Procedures”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: Do not use the engine exhaust or propeller as grounding points. Damage to the propeller can result, and there is no way of quickly ensuring a positive bond between the engine and the airframe.

notes.front: By what two methods can an aircraft be defuelled?
notes.back: Gravity defuelling, or pumping the fuel out of the tanks.
notes.explanation: Procedures differ between aircraft types, and the handbook says to check the maintenance/service manual first.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Defueling”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: Defueling procedures differ with different types of aircraft. Before defueling an aircraft, check the maintenance/service manual for specific procedures and cautions. Defueling can be accomplished by gravity defueling or by pumping the fuel out of the tanks.

notes.front: Fuel pumped out of a wing tank for a repair is to be poured back into the airport’s main storage tank of good fuel. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) The removed fuel cannot be mixed with good fuel
B) It may be mixed after the sumps are drained
C) It may be mixed if the aircraft was grounded
D) It may be mixed if it is the same grade
notes.back: A) The removed fuel cannot be mixed with good fuel
notes.choicesExplained: D: the handbook gives no same-grade exception. B: draining sumps is a pre-fuelling check, not a licence to mix. C: grounding is a safety precaution, unrelated to fuel quality.
notes.explanation: The handbook says fuel removed by pumping cannot be mixed with good fuel, and the tanks must not be damaged in the process.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Defueling”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: When the pumping method is used, care must be taken not to damage the tanks, and the removed fuel cannot be mixed with good fuel.

notes.front: Among the general precautions when defuelling: have the correct type of {{c1::fire extinguisher}} available, and wear eye protection.
notes.explanation: Both sit in the handbook’s list of general precautions for defuelling.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Defueling”, p. 1-28
notes.evidence: Have the correct type of fire extinguisher available. • Wear eye protection.

notes.front: Which ACS subject area has a knowledge element on tool and hardware use and accountability?
notes.back: General Subject F, Ground Operations and Servicing.
notes.explanation: In the same list it is followed by the elements on material handling and on parts protections.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), I.F Ground Operations and Servicing, p. 9
notes.evidence: AM.I.F.K12 Tool and hardware use and accountability. AM.I.F.K13 Material handling. AM.I.F.K14 Parts protections.

notes.front: After an intake inspection on a turbine engine, a mechanic’s toolbox is one screwdriver short. The engine is due for a ground run. Which handbook point applies most directly?
notes.choices:
A) The starter duty cycle
B) Tool control and never leaving tools around a turbine intake
C) The risk diamond for hazardous materials
D) The rule on tie-down stakes
notes.back: B) Tool control and never leaving tools around a turbine intake
notes.choicesExplained: A: the duty cycle protects the starter from overheating. C: the risk diamond labels hazardous materials. D: stakes concern securing parked aircraft.
notes.explanation: A tool left near the intake can be drawn in by the low-pressure area in front of the engine; tool control is one of the handbook’s FOD controls.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B), ch. 1, “Foreign Object Damage (FOD)”, p. 1-4
notes.evidence: To control FOD, keep ramp and operation areas clean, have a tool control program, and provide convenient receptacles for used hardware, shop towels, and other consumables. Never leave tools or other items around the intake of a turbine engine.

notes.front: In ACS Ground Operations and Servicing, which two knowledge elements come straight after tool and hardware use and accountability?
notes.back: Material handling, then parts protections.
notes.explanation: The element after them covers hazardous materials, Safety Data Sheets and personal protective equipment.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), I.F Ground Operations and Servicing, p. 9
notes.evidence: AM.I.F.K12 Tool and hardware use and accountability. AM.I.F.K13 Material handling. AM.I.F.K14 Parts protections. AM.I.F.K15 Hazardous materials, Safety Data Sheets (SDS), and PPE.
